title: AI Agents / Agentic AI
blurb: LLMs that take actions — tool use, planning, guardrails, multi-step workflows, and Model Context Protocol (MCP).

beginner: What an agent is (vs a chatbot)

lessons.title: The agent loop
lessons.explain: An agent is an LLM in a loop: it observes state, decides an action (often calling a tool), executes it, sees the result, and repeats until the task is done. Tools give it the ability to DO things, not just talk.
lessons.example:
while not done:
    action = llm(state, tools)
    result = run(action)
    state = update(state, result)
objectives: Describe the observe-decide-act cycle an agent runs

lessons.title: Tool use & function calling
objectives: Explain how an LLM invokes external tools via function calling
Explain how function calling changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect function calling with tool definitions and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Tool use is what turns an LLM from 'a text generator' into 'a system that can act.' Function calling gives the model a defined list of available tools (name, description, expected arguments) and lets it choose to output a structured request to call one — your code executes the actual function and returns the result back to the model for the next step.
commonMistakes: Assuming the model directly executes actions itself — it only ever outputs a structured REQUEST to call a tool; your application code is what actually performs the action, which is exactly.
lessons.careerRelevance: Function calling is the specific mechanism underlying essentially every real AI agent product today.

lessons.title: Memory in agent systems
objectives: Distinguish short-term and long-term memory in an agent system
Explain how short-term memory changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect short-term memory with long-term memory and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Short-term memory is simply the current conversation/task context within the active context window — it disappears once the session ends.
examples:
# short-term: 'the user just said they prefer bullet points' -- lives only in this conversation's context
# long-term: 'this user has consistently preferred bullet points across the last 20 sessions'
# -- stored externally, retrieved and injected into context when a new session starts
commonMistakes: Assuming an agent 'remembers' anything between separate sessions without an explicit external memory system — without one, every new session starts with a genuinely blank context.
lessons.careerRelevance: Memory design is a core, practical architecture decision in any agent meant to improve over repeated use, not a solved default.

lessons.title: Planning, reflection & verification
objectives: Explain how agents break down goals into steps and check their own work
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: ReAct reasoning-and-action pattern.
Explain how planning changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect planning with reflection and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Planning is breaking a high-level goal ('book me the cheapest flight under $500') into a concrete sequence of steps (search flights, filter by price, check availability, confirm).
examples:
# planning: goal -> [search_flights(), filter(price<500), sort(cheapest), confirm_with_user()]
# reflection: after search_flights() returns results, agent checks 'do these actually match the constraints?'
# before proceeding, rather than blindly trusting the first result
commonMistakes: Skipping reflection entirely for cost/speed and just chaining steps blindly — this works fine for simple, low-stakes tasks but is risky for anything where an intermediate error could.
lessons.careerRelevance: Planning and reflection quality is exactly what separates a genuinely useful agent from one that confidently takes a wrong action. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Human approval, permissions & least privilege
objectives: Design appropriate human-approval gates and permission scoping for an agent
Explain how human-in-the-loop approval changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect human-in-the-loop approval with least privilege and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Not every agent action should execute automatically — high-stakes or irreversible actions (sending an email, making a purchase, deleting data) should typically require human approval before executing, especially early in a system's deployment.
examples:
# a research agent needs: web search, document read access
# a research agent does NOT need: ability to send emails, delete files, or make purchases
# -- scope its tool access to exactly what the task requires, nothing more
commonMistakes: Giving an agent broad tool access 'to be flexible for future tasks' — this directly increases the blast radius of any single agent mistake or adversarial prompt injection.
lessons.careerRelevance: Approval gates and least-privilege scoping are the most important practical safety controls in any real production agent system.

lessons.title: Error handling, recovery & agent evaluation
objectives: Design error recovery for agent tool failures and evaluate agent performance
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: agent task-completion rate, agent latency and tool-call observability.
Explain how error recovery changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect error recovery with retry/fallback strategies and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Tool calls fail — APIs time out, return unexpected data, or reject invalid input — and an agent needs an explicit strategy: retry, fall back to an alternative approach, or surface the failure clearly rather than silently proceeding with bad data.
commonMistakes: Letting an agent silently continue after a failed tool call as if it had succeeded — this can compound into a confidently wrong final action built on a foundation that already failed.
lessons.careerRelevance: Robust error handling is what separates a demo-quality agent from one trustworthy enough for real production use. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.
lessons.explain: Tool calls fail — APIs time out, return unexpected data, or reject invalid input — and an agent needs an explicit strategy: retry, fall back to an alternative approach, or surface the failure clearly rather than silently proceeding with bad data.

lessons.title: Security risks & when not to use agents
objectives: Identify agent-specific security risks and recognize when a simpler system is the better choice
Explain how injection-driven tool misuse changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect injection-driven tool misuse with blast radius of tool access and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Agents introduce risks beyond a normal LLM call: prompt injection can hijack an agent's tool-use decisions (not just its text output), and a compromised or confused agent with real tool access can take real, damaging actions — not just generate bad text.
examples:
# a task that ALWAYS does: fetch data -> transform -> save --
# with no real decisions or branching needed -- is better as a simple script,
# NOT an agent; agents earn their complexity cost when genuine judgment/adaptation is needed
concepts: when a script beats an agent
commonMistakes: Defaulting to an agentic architecture for any automation task, regardless of whether real decision-making is actually involved — this adds cost, latency, and failure surface for no real.
lessons.careerRelevance: Knowing when NOT to use an agent is just as valuable an architecture skill as knowing how to build one well, and is a common senior-level interview distinction.

lessons.title: When an agent is the right tool
objectives: Decide when agent overhead is actually justified
Explain how when to use an agent changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect when to use an agent with fixed script vs dynamic decisions and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: An agent is justified when a task genuinely requires multiple dynamic steps, tool calls, and decisions that can't be predetermined in a fixed script. For tasks with a known, fixed sequence of steps, a simple deterministic script is more reliable, cheaper, and easier to debug than an agent.
examples:
# good agent fit: 'research this topic, decide which sources are credible,
# then summarize' -- the STEPS aren't knowable in advance
# poor agent fit: 'always run steps A, B, then C in that exact order' --
# just write a script; an agent adds cost and unpredictability with no benefit
commonMistakes: Building an agent for a task with a known, fixed sequence of steps, when a simple deterministic script would be more reliable and far cheaper.
lessons.careerRelevance: Correctly scoping when agent overhead is justified is a genuinely important, practical architecture decision.
lessons.explain: An agent is justified when a task genuinely requires multiple dynamic steps, tool calls, and decisions that can't be predetermined in a fixed script. lessons.title: MCP: why it exists & host/client/server architecture
objectives: Explain how MCP standardizes connections between LLM applications and external context/tools.
Explain how MCP changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect MCP with host and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Model Context Protocol separates an AI host application, MCP clients managed by that host, and MCP servers that expose capabilities. The protocol reduces one-off integration code by standardizing discovery and invocation of tools, resources, prompts, and client-side features.
lessons.explain: Model Context Protocol separates an AI host application, MCP clients managed by that host, and MCP servers that expose capabilities. The protocol reduces one-off integration code by standardizing discovery and invocation of tools, resources, prompts, and client-side features.
examples:
architecture={"host":"assistant app","client":"MCP connection","server":"calendar/files service"}
print(architecture)
lessons.example:
architecture={"host":"assistant app","client":"MCP connection","server":"calendar/files service"}
print(architecture)
commonMistakes: Calling MCP “a model” or “an agent” confuses the protocol layer with the application and reasoning layers built on top of it.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in real engineering design, debugging, review, or production work and is useful in technical interviews.

lessons.title: Base protocol, JSON-RPC, lifecycle & capabilities
objectives: Trace initialization and capability negotiation before normal requests begin.
Explain how JSON-RPC changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect JSON-RPC with initialize and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: MCP messages use JSON-RPC 2.0 and a defined lifecycle. Client and server initialize the connection, exchange protocol versions and capability declarations, then perform capability-specific requests.
lessons.explain: MCP messages use JSON-RPC 2.0 and a defined lifecycle. Client and server initialize the connection, exchange protocol versions and capability declarations, then perform capability-specific requests.
examples:
message={"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"current"}}
print(message["method"])
lessons.example:
message={"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"current"}}

commonMistakes: Sending tool or resource requests before initialization/capability negotiation can make implementations fail unpredictably across clients.

lessons.title: Transports: stdio & Streamable HTTP
objectives: Choose a transport based on local process versus remote service boundaries.
Explain how stdio changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect stdio with Streamable HTTP and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: MCP can run over transports such as stdio for a locally launched server process or Streamable HTTP for networked services. Stdio is simple and keeps credentials in the local process environment; HTTP introduces network authentication, server discovery, scaling, and failure concerns.
lessons.explain: MCP can run over transports such as stdio for a locally launched server process or Streamable HTTP for networked services. Stdio is simple and keeps credentials in the local process environment; HTTP introduces network authentication, server discovery, scaling, and failure concerns.
lessons.example:

commonMistakes: Treating stdout as a place for arbitrary debug printing in a stdio server can corrupt the protocol message stream; logs belong on stderr or another channel.

lessons.title: Tools: schemas, discovery & safe invocation
objectives: Expose model-invokable actions with clear schemas and application-controlled safety.
Explain how tools changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect tools with JSON schema and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: MCP tools are server capabilities that models may discover and request to invoke. A tool definition needs a precise name, description, and input schema so the model can construct valid arguments.
lessons.explain: MCP tools are server capabilities that models may discover and request to invoke. A tool definition needs a precise name, description, and input schema so the model can construct valid arguments.
examples:

print(tool)
lessons.example:
tool={"name":"get_weather","inputSchema":{"type":"object","required":["city"]}}
print(tool)
commonMistakes: Trusting model-generated tool arguments without server-side validation can turn a harmless-looking tool call into an invalid or unsafe operation.

lessons.title: Resources: exposing contextual data

Explain how resources changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect resources with URI and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Resources provide application-controlled contextual data such as files, database records, repository history, or documentation. Servers can expose concrete resource URIs and templates for parameterized resources.
lessons.explain: Resources provide application-controlled contextual data such as files, database records, repository history, or documentation. Servers can expose concrete resource URIs and templates for parameterized resources.

lessons.explanation: MCP prompts are reusable templates a server exposes for explicit user selection. They may accept arguments and return structured messages or embedded resources.
lessons.explain: MCP prompts are reusable templates a server exposes for explicit user selection. They may accept arguments and return structured messages or embedded resources.
examples:

lessons.title: Client features: sampling, roots & elicitation
objectives: Explain capabilities that servers may request from the client/host side.
Explain how sampling changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect sampling with roots and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: MCP is bidirectional: clients can expose features to servers. Sampling lets a server request model generation through the host under host/user controls; roots describe filesystem or URI boundaries the client makes available; elicitation lets a server request additional user information.
lessons.explain: MCP is bidirectional: clients can expose features to servers. Sampling lets a server request model generation through the host under host/user controls; roots describe filesystem or URI boundaries the client makes available; elicitation lets a server request additional user information.

lessons.example:

lessons.explanation: A maintainable server keeps protocol registration thin and places real business logic in ordinary functions that can be unit tested without an MCP client. Tool/resource schemas should be narrow, deterministic where possible, and explicit about errors.

Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Remote MCP authorization follows modern OAuth-based patterns. The client discovers authorization metadata, obtains an access token intended for the specific MCP resource, and sends it in the Authorization header.
lessons.explain: Remote MCP authorization follows modern OAuth-based patterns. The client discovers authorization metadata, obtains an access token intended for the specific MCP resource, and sends it in the Authorization header.
examples:

lessons.example:

commonMistakes: Token passthrough to an unrelated downstream API can expose credentials to the wrong audience and violates the intended authorization boundary.

lessons.title: MCP security, consent & trust boundaries
objectives: Design MCP integrations assuming server data and tool descriptions can be untrusted.
Explain how consent changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect consent with tool safety and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: MCP enables data access and code-execution paths, so hosts need explicit consent, clear capability visibility, least privilege, input/output validation, and isolation for risky operations. Resource content or tool descriptions may contain malicious or misleading instructions; the host should not treat server-provided text as trusted policy.
lessons.explain: MCP enables data access and code-execution paths, so hosts need explicit consent, clear capability visibility, least privilege, input/output validation, and isolation for risky operations. Resource content or tool descriptions may contain malicious or misleading instructions; the host should not treat server-provided text as trusted policy.
examples:

lessons.example:

lessons.explanation: Production protocol integrations need predictable errors, cancellation, timeouts, progress signals, logs, and compatibility tests. JSON-RPC errors should distinguish invalid requests from application failures, long-running operations should respect cancellation, and logs must not corrupt transport streams or expose secrets.
lessons.explain: Production protocol integrations need predictable errors, cancellation, timeouts, progress signals, logs, and compatibility tests. JSON-RPC errors should distinguish invalid requests from application failures, long-running operations should respect cancellation, and logs must not corrupt transport streams or expose secrets.

only used during training, never inference

quiz.q: What distinguishes a multi-agent system from a single-agent workflow?
options: there's no real difference
multiple specialized agents collaborate, each often handling a distinct role, versus one agent handling everything
multi-agent systems never communicate with each other
single-agent workflows always perform better

quiz.q: What is coordination overhead in multi-agent systems?
options: a benefit with no downsides
the added complexity and cost of managing communication and hand-offs between multiple agents
a synonym for memory persistence
only relevant for single-agent systems

quiz.q: Why include human-in-the-loop approval for certain agent actions?
options: approval steps are always unnecessary friction
some actions are irreversible or high-stakes enough that a human check before execution reduces real risk
human approval only applies to low-stakes actions
this concept doesn't apply to real agent systems

quiz.q: What does 'least privilege' mean for an agent's tool access?
options: giving an agent access to every possible tool
granting only the minimum permissions/tools actually needed for its task, limiting potential damage from mistakes or misuse
least privilege means no tools at all
privilege level has no security relevance

quiz.q: Why gate irreversible actions (like deleting data) more strictly than reversible ones?
options: irreversible actions need no special handling
a mistake on an irreversible action can't simply be undone, so extra caution (like approval) reduces real, permanent harm
all actions carry identical risk
gating irreversible actions is only relevant for financial systems

quiz.q: What is a retry/fallback strategy in agent error handling?
options: ignoring all errors permanently
having a defined response when a step fails, like retrying, trying an alternative approach, or escalating to a human
a synonym for planning
only relevant during training

quiz.q: Why is end-to-end task evaluation important for agents, not just per-step correctness?
options: per-step correctness is always sufficient
an agent can execute each individual step 'correctly' yet still fail to accomplish the actual overall goal
end-to-end evaluation is never practical for agents
this only matters for single-step tasks

quiz.q: What is injection-driven tool misuse?
options: a hardware failure
malicious input tricking an agent into misusing its available tools in unintended, potentially harmful ways
a synonym for reflection
only a risk for agents with no tool access

quiz.q: What does 'blast radius of tool access' refer to?
options: the physical location of a server
how much potential damage an agent could cause given the tools and permissions it has access to
a synonym for context window
irrelevant to agent security

quiz.q: When does 'a script beat an agent'?
options: scripts are never a better choice than agents
when the task follows a fixed, predictable sequence of steps that doesn't require dynamic, model-driven decisions
scripts always underperform agents regardless of task
this comparison doesn't apply in practice

quiz.q: What is the agent loop, at a high level?
options: a single one-shot model call with no iteration
a repeating cycle of observing state, deciding an action (often via a tool), executing it, and incorporating the result before deciding the next step
a synonym for training loop specifically for language models
only relevant for image-generating systems

quiz.q: What does 'planning' mean in an agentic system?
options: executing actions with no forethought
the agent determining a sequence of steps likely to accomplish a goal before or while acting
a synonym for memory
only relevant for multi-agent systems

quiz.q: Why might an agent need to dynamically re-plan mid-task?
options: re-planning is never necessary
new information or a failed step can invalidate the original plan, requiring the agent to adjust course
plans are always followed exactly regardless of outcomes
re-planning only applies during training

quiz.q: What risk does giving an agent broad, unrestricted tool access create?
options: no meaningful risk if the model is capable enough
a larger blast radius -- more potential for a mistake or manipulated input to cause significant, hard-to-reverse damage
broad access always improves task performance with no trade-offs
this risk only applies to multi-agent systems

quiz.q: Why might state tracking be necessary within a single agent task?
options: state tracking is never necessary
the agent needs to remember what it has already done and observed within the task to make sensible next decisions
state is irrelevant to agent decision-making
state only matters across separate sessions, never within one task

quiz.q: What is a practical reason to prefer a deterministic script over an agent for a fixed, simple task?
options: scripts are always worse for every task
reliability, cost, and predictability -- an agent adds unpredictability and expense with no benefit when the steps are already fully known
agents are always cheaper to run than scripts
there's no practical reason, agents are strictly superior

quiz.q: Why might error recovery be more complex in an agent system than in a simple script?
options: it's equally simple in both cases
an agent's dynamic decision-making means failures can occur in many different, less predictable places compared to a fixed script's known steps
agents never encounter errors
scripts have no error handling capability at all

quiz.q: What is the practical value of logging an agent's tool calls and decisions?
options: logging has no practical value for agents
it enables debugging, auditing, and understanding why an agent took a particular action after the fact
logging only matters for training, not deployed agents
agents don't make discrete, loggable decisions

exercises.title: Define tools
exercises.prompt: For a research assistant agent, list 3 tools it would need.

exercises.title: Trace a loop
exercises.prompt: Walk through the agent loop for 'book me a flight under $500'.

exercises.title: Add guardrails
exercises.prompt: What guardrails stop an agent from taking harmful/expensive actions?

exercises.title: Trace a function call
exercises.prompt: Given a weather tool definition and a user asking about weather in Dubai, write out the model's tool-call request and what your code would return.

exercises.title: Short-term or long-term memory
exercises.prompt: For 3 given pieces of information (a user's stated preference for this session, a user's name, a fact just retrieved from a tool call), classify each as short-term or long-term memory.

exercises.title: Design a plan with reflection
exercises.prompt: For the goal 'find and summarize the 3 most relevant recent articles on a topic,' write out the step-by-step plan including one reflection checkpoint.

exercises.title: Scope least-privilege access
exercises.prompt: An agent's task is to answer questions about internal documentation. List the tools it should have access to, and 2 tools it explicitly should NOT have.

exercises.title: Design an approval gate
exercises.prompt: For an agent that can draft AND send customer emails, design the approval-gate policy: which actions need human approval and which can proceed automatically.

exercises.title: Agent or simple script
exercises.prompt: A task always follows the same fixed sequence: fetch a report, reformat it, email it every Monday. Argue whether this should be built as an agent or a simple script.

exercises.title: Design a tool definition
exercises.prompt: Design a function-calling tool definition for 'get current weather for a city' (name, parameters).

exercises.title: Choose single-agent or multi-agent
exercises.prompt: For a task needing research, writing, and fact-checking as distinct specialized roles, would single-agent or multi-agent fit better? Why.
exercises.hint: multi-agent -- distinct specialized roles benefit from separation of concerns

exercises.title: Design a human-approval gate
exercises.prompt: For an agent that can send emails on a user's behalf, describe where you'd add human-in-the-loop approval.
exercises.hint: before actually sending -- an irreversible, externally-visible action

exercises.title: Decide agent vs script
exercises.prompt: A task always runs the exact same 3 steps in the exact same order. Should this be an agent or a script?
exercises.hint: a script -- the steps are fixed and don't need dynamic decision-making
